analysis.one_liner: Raises car and truck fuel economy standards to 40 mpg and fixes how mileage is tested.
analysis.headline: The Automobile Fuel Efficiency Improvements Act of 2003 was introduced in the Senate by Sen. Durbin with 9 cosponsors and never received a hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Commerce Committee when the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have phased in steadily higher mileage requirements for cars and for larger vehicles like many SUVs and pickups, raising the car standard from 25 to 40 miles per gallon by model year 2015 and the truck standard from 17 to 27.5. It would have doubled the fine automakers pay for violating the standards, brought big SUVs under the mileage rules by raising the weight limits that currently exempt them, ordered more accurate mileage testing so stickers match real-world driving, and required federal agencies to buy more fuel-efficient vehicles. It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Car buyers and households that drive, who would have saved money at the pump as new vehicles used less gasoline, and communities affected by auto emissions. Taxpayers also benefit from reduced oil demand pressures; the federal government fleet savings too.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the passenger-car fuel economy standard in steps from 25 miles per gallon to 40 miles per gallon for model years after 2014, and the standard for other automobiles (covering many SUVs and pickups) from 17 to 27.5 miles per gallon.

Raises the weight threshold in the definitions of automobile and passenger automobile from 6,000 to 12,000 pounds and other limits to 14,000 pounds, bringing heavier vehicles that were previously exempt into the fuel economy program.

Directs the Volpe National Transportation Systems Center to study how to make fuel economy testing match real-world highway and city driving, and requires revised testing so that stated mileage is accurate, without allowing standards to become weaker in the process.
Doubles the civil penalty for violating fuel economy standards from $5 to $10 per mile-per-gallon shortfall and indexes it to inflation.

Requires executive agencies to meet fleet mileage standards and to lease or buy a minimum share of exceptionally fuel-efficient vehicles, including at least 10,000 such vehicles in the fleet beginning in fiscal year 2009.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, who would need to redesign vehicles and sell more fuel-efficient cars and trucks, and potentially buyers of large, fuel-hungry vehicles, who could face higher sticker prices or fewer choices of very large SUVs. Oil companies would face weaker gasoline demand.

drawbacks.text: Tightening mileage standards can raise the upfront price of new vehicles, and critics argued it constrains the availability of large SUVs and pickups, a burden that falls hardest on buyers of those vehicles even as it lowers fuel spending over time.

The bill relies on the existing Corporate Average Fuel Economy structure, which lets manufacturers average across their fleets and could concentrate compliance costs on specific models rather than guaranteeing every vehicle improves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is higher engineering and vehicle costs for automakers and some higher sticker prices for buyers of large vehicles, set against lower gasoline bills for every driver, reduced oil consumption, and more honest mileage labels. The phase-in over roughly a decade gives manufacturers time to adjust, and the bill requires that revised testing not weaken the standards. The main honest objection is cost and choice at the showroom, not that the public loses overall.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2003 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005 without any hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill on April 7, 2003, with initial cosponsors including Sens. Nelson of Florida, Jeffords, Corzine, Reed, Kennedy, and Boxer.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
Sen. Durbin delivered introductory remarks again on March 31, 2004, apparently seeking attention for the bill.
No further action was taken; the bill never left committee and received no vote before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers and oil companies were better off because the bill never became law, avoiding higher mileage requirements and larger fines. Vehicle buyers continued to pay for more gasoline than they would have under the higher standards.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Automobile Fuel Efficiency Improvements Act of 2003 and later delivered additional introductory remarks in March 2004.

for.name: Sens. Bill Nelson (FL), Jim Jeffords, Jon Corzine, Jack Reed, Edward Kennedy, and Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction (Jeffords listed as Independent).

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out or held a vote.

against.name: Automakers
against.what_they_did: The bill's higher mileage standards and doubled fines directly targeted automakers, and the broader pushback against raising CAFE standards in the early 2000s was heavily driven by the industry.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats plus one Independent; no Republicans signed on, and the bill died in committee without a floor vote that would have revealed broader positioning.

industries.note: The bill would have forced automakers to raise fleet mileage to 40 mpg for cars and 27.5 for trucks, double fines for noncompliance, and bring heavy SUVs into the program, requiring costly redesigns. Consumers would have recouped those costs through lower fuel spending.
Higher mileage standards reduce gasoline consumption, cutting into fuel sales. Every dollar saved at the pump is a dollar not spent on gasoline.
Bringing heavier vehicles under the mileage rules could raise prices or limit choices for buyers of very large vehicles, while lowering operating costs for everyone who drives.
